stem: Ananya's block on a spring slides on a smooth table between extreme points P and Q, 12 cm apart. She released it from P. When the block is 2 cm from P, what are the amplitude and the magnitude of its displacement?

options.A: Amplitude 12 cm, displacement 4 cm
options.B: Amplitude 6 cm, displacement 4 cm
options.C: Amplitude 6 cm, displacement 2 cm
options.D: Amplitude 6 cm, displacement 8 cm

r1.text: The mean position is exactly in the middle of P and Q, so amplitude is half of 12 cm and displacement is counted from the middle.

r2.text: Amplitude is how far it goes in total, from P all the way to Q.

r3.text: It started from P, so how far it has moved from P is its displacement.

calc: A = 0.12/2 = 0.06 m; mean is 0.06 m from P; |x| = 0.06 - 0.02 = 0.04 m. SLIP D: added instead of subtracted, 0.06 + 0.02 = 0.08 m.

steps.text: Amplitude: the extremes are 12 cm apart, so A = 12 ÷ 2 = 6 cm.
steps.trap_text: taking the full 12 cm between the extremes as the amplitude.

steps.text: Mean position: halfway between P and Q, so 6 cm from P. Displacement is measured from here.
steps.trap_text: measuring displacement from P, where it started, instead of from the mean (giving 2 cm).

steps.text: Displacement: the block is 2 cm from P, so |x| = 6 − 2 = 4 cm.
steps.trap_text: adding instead of subtracting: 6 + 2 = 8 cm.

verify_flags: Option A pairs S1 amplitude with the correct displacement; reviewer to confirm an S1 student would still place the mean midway.

stem: In a Nashik park, Priya's swing moves between two extreme points that are 1.6 m apart, with small swings. Which statement about the swing is correct?

options.A: Its amplitude is 1.6 m, the distance from one extreme to the other
options.B: Its displacement at any instant is measured from the point where Priya was let go
options.C: Its amplitude is 0.8 m, measured from the lowest point to either extreme
options.D: Because it repeats regularly, it is SHM even for very large swings

r1.text: The swing keeps going back and forth at regular intervals, so it has to be SHM, whatever the size of swing.

r2.text: Amplitude is the biggest distance from the lowest point, which is half the end-to-end gap.

r3.text: Amplitude is the whole width of the swing, front end to back end.

calc: A = 1.6/2 = 0.8 m (distance measured along the arc for small swings).

steps.text: Mean position: the lowest point, midway between the two extremes. Displacement is measured from here.
steps.trap_text: measuring displacement from the point where Priya was let go instead of from the lowest point.

steps.text: Amplitude: the extremes are 1.6 m apart, so A = 1.6 ÷ 2 = 0.8 m.
steps.trap_text: taking the full 1.6 m between the extremes as the amplitude.

steps.text: SHM: this works because the swings are small. Very large swings still repeat, but they are not SHM.
steps.trap_text: thinking anything that repeats regularly is SHM, whatever the size of the swing.

verify_flags: Option D relies on 'large-angle pendulum is periodic but not SHM'; confirm this is within HSC scope.

stem: In a tailoring shop in Solapur, a sewing-machine needle tip moves up and down, approximately in SHM, between 2 mm below the needle plate and 14 mm above it. What are its amplitude and mean position?

options.A: Amplitude 16 mm; mean position 6 mm above the plate
options.B: Amplitude 8 mm; displacement measured from the topmost point, 14 mm above the plate
options.C: Amplitude 6 mm; mean position 8 mm above the plate
options.D: Amplitude 8 mm; mean position 6 mm above the plate

r1.text: The full stroke is 14 + 2 = 16 mm, the mean is the midpoint of the stroke, so the amplitude is half of it.

r2.text: The amplitude is just the full stroke of the needle, top to bottom.

r3.text: The needle starts its stroke from the top, so displacement should be counted from there.

calc: Stroke = 0.014 - (-0.002) = 0.016 m; A = 0.008 m; mean = (0.014 + (-0.002))/2 = 0.006 m above plate. SLIP C: sign dropped, 14 - 2 = 12 mm, A = 6 mm, mean 8 mm.

steps.text: Positions: top = +14 mm, bottom = −2 mm (below the plate), so the stroke is 14 − (−2) = 16 mm.
steps.trap_text: dropping the minus sign on the bottom point: 14 − 2 = 12 mm, which gives an amplitude of 6 mm.

steps.text: Amplitude: half the stroke, A = 16 ÷ 2 = 8 mm.
steps.trap_text: taking the full 16 mm stroke as the amplitude.

steps.text: Mean position: the midpoint, (14 + (−2)) ÷ 2 = 6 mm above the plate. Displacement is measured from here.
steps.trap_text: measuring displacement from the topmost point, where the stroke starts, instead of from the mean.

verify_flags: Real sewing-machine needle motion is only approximately SHM (crank-driven); stem says 'approximately'.

stem: Kavya pulls a block on a spring to one end of a smooth table and lets it go. At which point in its motion is the block's displacement zero? Give a reason.
answer_key: Displacement is zero at the mean (equilibrium) position, midway between the two extremes.
expected_reasoning: Displacement in an oscillation is measured from the mean position, where the spring is at its natural length and the net force is zero; the release point is only an extreme, at x = +A.

follow_ups.S3: If Kavya released the block from the opposite end instead, would the point of zero displacement move? Why?
follow_ups.CORRECT_NO_REASON: Why is that point, and not the release point, used as the reference for displacement?
follow_ups.CORRECT: At the point where displacement is zero, what can you say about the block's speed and its acceleration?
follow_ups.UNCLEAR: Which place do you mean: the end where she let go, the opposite end, or somewhere between them?

steps.text: Release point: she let go at one end, so that point is an extreme, x = +A. It is where the motion starts, not where displacement is zero.
steps.trap_text: taking the release point as zero displacement because that's where it started.

steps.text: Reference: displacement is measured from the mean position, midway between the two ends, where the spring is at its natural length and the net force is zero. So x = 0 there.
steps.trap_text: measuring displacement from an end of the motion instead of from the mean.

verify_flags: A correct answer such as 'at the middle, not at the end' contains both 'middle' and 'at the end'; the engine must resolve this overlap (e.g., negation handling or accept_any priority).

stem: In the physics lab, a block on a spring oscillates on a smooth table. The two extreme positions are 10 cm apart. What is the amplitude in metres? Say how you got it.
answer_key: The amplitude is 0.05 m, half the distance between the two extremes.
expected_reasoning: The mean position is midway between the extremes and amplitude is the maximum displacement from the mean, so A = 0.10 m / 2 = 0.05 m.

slips.why: used peak-to-peak distance between the extremes as amplitude
gave the value in cm instead of metres

follow_ups.S1: If the amplitude really were 10 cm, how far from the mean position would each extreme be, and how far apart would the two extremes be?
follow_ups.CORRECT_NO_REASON: Why do you take half of the 10 cm rather than the whole 10 cm?
follow_ups.CORRECT: When the block is 3 cm from one extreme, what is its displacement from the mean position, in metres?
follow_ups.UNCLEAR: What number did you get for the amplitude, and in which unit?

half.text: took the full distance between the extremes as the amplitude

alternatives.text: halved twice

steps.text: Mean position: midway between the extremes. Amplitude is measured from there, so it is half the gap.
steps.trap_text: taking the full distance between the extremes as the amplitude.

steps.text: Units: the gap is 10 cm = 0.10 m.
steps.trap_text: staying in centimetres and answering 5 instead of 0.05 m.

steps.text: Amplitude: A = 0.10 ÷ 2 = 0.05 m.
steps.trap_text: leaving out the ÷ 2 and giving the whole 0.10 m.

steps.text: Check: 0.05 m out from the mean on each side, and 0.05 + 0.05 = 0.10 m, the full gap.
steps.trap_text: halving a second time and getting 0.025 m.

verify_flags: S1 phrase 'full distance' may appear in a correct answer like 'half of the full distance'; numeric value should take priority.

stem: Which statement about oscillating bodies is correct?

options.A: A block on a spring oscillates about its mean position, where the net force on it is zero, and its displacement is measured from that position
options.B: A ball bouncing up and down on the floor is in SHM, because it repeats at equal time intervals
options.C: The amplitude of a pendulum is the distance between its two extreme positions
options.D: The displacement of a pendulum bob is measured from the point where it was released

r1.text: Everything is measured from the mean position because that is where the net force is zero.

r2.text: Anything that repeats regularly, like a bouncing ball, is SHM.

r3.text: Amplitude means the full width of the swing from one end to the other.

stem: Aarav says a ball bouncing straight up and down on the floor is in SHM because it repeats at equal time intervals. Is he right?

options.A: Yes; any motion that repeats at equal time intervals is SHM
options.B: No; it is periodic, but the force on the ball in the air is a constant mg, not a restoring force proportional to its displacement from a mean position
options.C: Yes; the ball keeps coming back to the floor, so the floor is its mean position
options.D: No; it is not periodic at all, because each bounce takes a different time

r1.text: SHM needs a force that pulls back toward a mean position and grows with the distance from it; in the air the ball only feels a constant mg.

r2.text: It repeats again and again at equal intervals, and that is exactly what SHM means.

r3.text: It goes up and comes back down the same way every time, so it has to be simple harmonic.

verify_flags: 'mg' in reasoning_any is a short token; check substring matching does not fire on unrelated words.

stem: Aarav's block, attached to a spring on a frictionless track, oscillates between x = −A and x = +A. Which statement is correct at the instant the block is at x = +A?

options.A: Its speed is the largest, because it is farthest from the centre.
options.B: Its speed is zero and its acceleration is also zero.
options.C: Its speed is zero and its acceleration is the largest, pointing toward x = 0.
options.D: Its speed is the same as at x = 0, because the motion repeats evenly.

r1.text: At the end the spring is stretched the most, so it pulls back hardest. The block stops for a moment but the pull is biggest there.

r2.text: The block has stopped at the end, so nothing is changing at that moment. No velocity means no acceleration.

r3.text: The end is the farthest point from the middle, so that is where the block is going the fastest.

steps.text: Speed at x = +A: the block turns around there, so it is at rest for an instant, v = 0.
steps.trap_text: thinking the speed is largest at the extreme because it is farthest from the centre.

steps.text: Compare with x = 0: the block is fastest at the mean, so the speed is not the same at x = +A and x = 0.
steps.trap_text: thinking the speed is the same everywhere because the motion repeats evenly.

steps.text: Acceleration: a = −ω²x is largest in size at x = +A, pointing toward x = 0.
steps.trap_text: thinking zero speed means zero acceleration.

stem: Sneha pulls a simple pendulum bob aside by a small angle and releases it. At the instant the bob is at the end of its swing, which statement is correct?

options.A: Speed is zero; acceleration is the largest and points toward the lowest point.
options.B: Speed is zero, so acceleration is also zero, because the bob is momentarily at rest.
options.C: Acceleration is the smallest here, because acceleration is greatest at the lowest point.
options.D: Speed is zero; acceleration is the largest and points away from the lowest point.

r1.text: At the end the bob is displaced the most, so the restoring pull back toward the bottom is strongest, even though it is stopped for an instant.

r2.text: The bob is not moving at the end, so there is nothing to accelerate it there.

r3.text: At the bottom the bob is moving fastest, so that is where its acceleration must be the biggest.

steps.text: Speed: at the end of the swing the bob turns around, so v = 0 for an instant. Zero speed doesn't mean zero acceleration.
steps.trap_text: thinking the bob is at rest, so its acceleration is zero too.

steps.text: Size: for small angles a = −ω²x, so the acceleration is largest where the displacement is largest, at the end, and zero at the lowest point.
steps.trap_text: thinking acceleration is largest at the lowest point, where the bob is fastest.

steps.text: Direction: the minus sign in a = −ω²x means it points back toward the lowest point.
steps.trap_text: dropping the minus sign, so it points away from the lowest point.

verify_flags: Pendulum treated as small-angle SHM: at the extreme the acceleration is tangential (≈ g sinθ ≈ gθ) toward the mean; at the lowest point the centripetal term v²/L is ignored, as is standard for the SHM approximation.

stem: At a Pune workshop, a vibration-test table moves a loose coin back and forth in SHM. Friction must supply the coin's acceleration, so the coin slips first where the acceleration is largest. Where does it first slip?

options.A: At the mean position, because the table's acceleration is greatest there.
options.B: At the extreme positions, because the table's acceleration is greatest there.
options.C: Equally likely anywhere, because the table moves at a steady speed throughout.
options.D: At the mean position, because at the extremes the table is at rest and so has no acceleration.

r1.text: At the ends the table is farthest from the middle, so the restoring acceleration is biggest and friction has to work hardest there.

r2.text: The table is fastest in the middle, so that is where it accelerates the most and the coin will slide.

r3.text: At the ends the table stops, so there is no acceleration there and the coin is safe at the ends.

steps.text: Speed: the table is in SHM, not moving steadily. It is fastest at the mean and at rest for an instant at the extremes.
steps.trap_text: thinking the table moves at a steady speed, so the coin could slip anywhere.

steps.text: Acceleration: a = −ω²x, so its size grows with distance from the mean and is zero at the mean itself.
steps.trap_text: thinking acceleration is greatest at the mean, where the table is fastest.

steps.text: At the extremes x = ±A, so the acceleration is largest there even though the table is at rest. Friction has to work hardest there, so the coin slips first at the extremes.
steps.trap_text: thinking zero speed at the extremes means zero acceleration.

verify_flags: Transfer context: coin slips when the needed friction m·ω²|x| exceeds μs·m·g, which first happens at |x| = A. Assumes ideal SHM of the table.

stem: Where is the speed of an ideal simple harmonic oscillator maximum? Give a reason.
expected_reasoning: At the mean position the potential energy is zero, so all the energy is kinetic and the speed is greatest (v = Aω). The restoring force speeds the body up all the way to the mean and slows it down after.

follow_ups.S4: What happens to the oscillator's kinetic energy when it momentarily stops at an extreme position?
follow_ups.S5: Compare the speed at the mean position with the speed at an extreme position — are they equal?
follow_ups.CORRECT_NO_REASON: Why is the speed maximum there?
follow_ups.CORRECT: Where is the acceleration of the same oscillator greatest, and which way does it point?
follow_ups.UNCLEAR: Can you name the position — the mean position or an extreme position — where the oscillator moves fastest?

steps.text: At an extreme the oscillator stops for an instant to turn around: v = 0 and all its energy is potential.
steps.trap_text: thinking the speed is largest at the extreme, the point farthest from the centre.

steps.text: Toward the mean the restoring force speeds it up; past the mean it slows it down. So the speed is greatest at the mean, where PE = 0 and all the energy is kinetic (v = Aω).
steps.trap_text: thinking the speed is the same everywhere.

verify_flags: Keyword matching is substring-based: a correct answer that also says 'zero at the extreme position' will hit both accept_any and S4. Grader precedence must be decided (suggest: accept_any wins unless the S4 phrase is the stated answer).
'mean' could match filler like 'I mean'; acceptable risk for a demo.

stem: Riya pulls a block on a smooth spring to one side and lets go. At the instant it stops at the far end, is its acceleration zero? Give a reason.
answer_key: No — its acceleration is greatest at the extreme position and points toward the mean position.
expected_reasoning: At the extreme the displacement is largest, so the restoring force −kx and the acceleration −ω²x are largest. Zero velocity only means the block is turning around, not that nothing acts on it.

follow_ups.S6: If the acceleration were zero at that instant, what would the block do next — stay there or come back?
follow_ups.S7: At the mean position, how much is the spring stretched, and what force does it exert on the block?
follow_ups.CORRECT_NO_REASON: Why is the acceleration not zero there, even though the velocity is zero?
follow_ups.CORRECT: A ball thrown straight up stops at its highest point. Is its acceleration zero there? How is that like the block at the far end?
follow_ups.UNCLEAR: Is the acceleration at the far end zero or not, and which way does it point?

steps.text: Velocity: at the far end v = 0 for an instant. That only means the block is turning around, not that nothing acts on it.
steps.trap_text: thinking zero velocity means zero acceleration.

steps.text: Acceleration: the displacement is largest there, x = A, so F = −kx and a = −ω²x are largest, pointing toward the mean. So it is not zero.
steps.trap_text: thinking the acceleration is greatest at the mean, where the block is fastest.

verify_flags: 'yes' is a short S6 trigger and could fire on unrelated filler ('yes, so...'); review against real transcripts.
A correct answer that adds 'and it is zero at the mean' does not hit S6/S7 phrases, but 'it is zero' could appear in a correct answer referring to velocity; review precedence.

stem: A 0.2 kg block on a spring (k = 20 N/m) oscillates on a smooth floor with amplitude 0.1 m. What are its speed and acceleration magnitude as it passes the mean position?

options.A: v = 1 m/s, a = 10 m/s²
options.B: v = 0, a = 0, since the block is fastest only at x = ±0.1 m
options.D: v = 1 m/s, a = 0

r1.text: At the mean position the spring is not stretched, so there is no force and a = 0. All the energy is kinetic there, so v = Aω = 1 m/s.

r2.text: The block moves fastest at the centre, so its acceleration should be the biggest there too.

r3.text: Farthest from the centre it has the most energy of motion, so at the centre it is the slowest.

calc: ω = √(k/m) = √(20/0.2) = 10 rad/s; v_max = Aω = 0.1 × 10 = 1 m/s; a = −ω²x = 0 at x = 0. SLIP C uses ω = k/m = 100 (forgot the square root): 0.1 × 100 = 10 m/s. Option A uses a_max = ω²A = 10 m/s² at the wrong place.

stem: Kavya's block on a spring oscillates in SHM with amplitude 0.05 m and angular frequency 10 rad/s. What is its speed as it passes the mean position?

options.A: 0 m/s, because it moves fastest at the extreme positions
options.B: 5 m/s
options.C: 0.5 m/s, its maximum speed
options.D: The same as at every other point, since the speed in SHM does not change

r1.text: At the mean position all the energy is kinetic, so the speed is greatest there: v = Aω = 0.05 × 10 = 0.5 m/s.

r2.text: The block is fastest at the ends where it was pulled the most, so in the middle it is the slowest.

r3.text: In SHM the block keeps moving at the same speed back and forth; only its direction changes.

verify_flags: An answer of 0 m/s is the S4 misconception, not a slip; it is caught by text patterns, not numeric.slips. Confirm the numeric grader routes 0 to S4 or UNCLEAR.

stem: In the physics lab, Sneha hangs two pendulums with equal string lengths. Bob X is 50 g and is pulled to 3°; bob Y is 200 g and is pulled to 6° (both small). She releases them together. Which finishes 10 oscillations first?

options.A: X, because its swing is smaller so each oscillation is shorter
options.B: Y, because gravity pulls the heavier bob harder so it swings faster
options.C: Both finish together
options.D: X, because the lighter bob is easier to move back and forth

r1.text: Y swings through a bigger arc, so it has more distance to cover and takes more time.

r2.text: T = 2π√(L/g) has only length and g in it, and both have the same length, so the period is the same.

r3.text: The heavy bob gets pulled down with more force, so it comes back quicker.

calc: T = 2π√(L/g) for both; independent of bob mass and of small amplitude, so both finish 10 oscillations together.

steps.text: Formula: T = 2π√(L/g). Only length and g are in it, and both strings are the same length.
steps.trap_text: thinking the heavier (or lighter) bob swings faster; mass isn't in the formula.

steps.text: Amplitude: 3° and 6° are both small, so the different swings don't change T either. Both finish 10 oscillations together.
steps.trap_text: thinking the bigger swing takes longer for each oscillation.

verify_flags: Assumes negligible air drag on both bobs and both angles within the small-angle regime.

stem: Rohan's simple pendulum is 0.64 m long and swings with an amplitude of 3°. He restarts it at 6° (still small). Take g = π² m/s². What is the time period now?

r1.text: He doubled the swing, so the bob travels double the path and the period doubles too.

r2.text: Amplitude isn't in T = 2π√(L/g), so the period stays what it was for 3°.

r3.text: ω = √(g/L) and the period is just 1/ω, so I take one by omega.

twopi.text: used 1/ω instead of 2π/ω (treated ω like the frequency)

alternatives.text: assumed doubling the swing angle doubles the period

steps.text: Amplitude: for small swings the period doesn't depend on amplitude, so going from 3° to 6° changes nothing.
steps.trap_text: thinking a bigger swing takes longer, so doubling the period to 3.2 s.

steps.text: Formula: T = 2π√(L/g) = 2π√(0.64/π²).
steps.trap_text: using ω, or 1/ω, as if it were the period (1/ω ≈ 0.25 s).

steps.text: Square root: √(0.64/π²) = 0.8/π, so T = 2π × 0.8/π = 1.6 s.
steps.trap_text: forgetting the square root: 2π × 0.64/π² ≈ 0.41 s.

stem: An empty tempo bounces on its suspension springs with a period of 0.5 s. After loading sacks of onions at a Nashik market, its total mass becomes 4 times. Treating it as a spring–mass system, what is the new bounce period?

options.B: 0.5 s, because the springs, not the load, decide the period
options.D: 0.5 s on a smooth road, but longer when a speed breaker makes it bounce higher

r1.text: T = 2π√(m/k), so 4 times the mass gives √4 = 2 times the period.

r2.text: Mass only matters for weight; the bounce time depends on how stiff the spring is.

r3.text: A bigger bounce means the tempo goes up and down more, so it takes more time.

calc: T ∝ √m: T₂ = 0.5 × √4 = 1.0 s. SLIP (T ∝ m, forgot root): 0.5 × 4 = 2.0 s.

alternatives.text: decided the load can't change the period, only the springs can

steps.text: Spring–mass period: T = 2π√(m/k). The springs (k) are the same, so T ∝ √m.
steps.trap_text: thinking only the springs decide the period, so the load changes nothing (0.5 s).
forgetting the square root: 0.5 × 4 = 2.0 s.

steps.text: Bounce size (amplitude) isn't in T, so it is still 1.0 s over a speed breaker.
steps.trap_text: thinking a bigger bounce takes longer.

verify_flags: Real vehicle suspension has dampers and non-ideal springs; idealised as a single spring–mass system with k unchanged.

stem: Meera swaps her pendulum's brass bob for a heavier iron bob of the same size, keeps the string length the same, and pulls it a little further (still a small angle). Does the period change? Why?
answer_key: No, the period stays the same because T = 2π√(L/g) depends only on length and g.
expected_reasoning: For small angles the pendulum's period depends only on L and g; the bob's mass cancels out and amplitude does not appear in the formula.

follow_ups.S8: If the bob is pulled further, it has a longer path. What else changes about how fast it moves at the bottom?
follow_ups.S9: In T = 2π√(L/g), where would the bob's mass appear? What happens to m when you write F = ma for the bob?
follow_ups.CORRECT_NO_REASON: You said the period does not change. Which quantities does a simple pendulum's period actually depend on?
follow_ups.CORRECT: Meera now takes the same pendulum to a hill station where g is slightly smaller. Will the period increase, decrease or stay the same?
follow_ups.UNCLEAR: Will one oscillation of the new bob take more time, less time, or the same time as before?

steps.text: Formula: for small angles T = 2π√(L/g). Only length and g are in it, and the length is unchanged.
steps.trap_text: thinking the heavier iron bob changes the period; mass isn't in the formula.

steps.text: Amplitude: pulled a little further is still a small angle, so the bigger swing doesn't change T either. The period stays the same.
steps.trap_text: thinking the bigger swing takes longer for each oscillation.

verify_flags: Same-size bob chosen so air drag is comparable; real heavy vs light bobs differ slightly due to drag.

stem: A spring toy on Aditya's desk oscillates with angular frequency 10π rad/s. What is its time period? Give your value with the formula you used.
expected_reasoning: Angular frequency ω is 2π times the frequency, so T = 2π/ω, not 1/ω; this gives f = 5 Hz and T = 0.2 s.

slips.why: used T = 1/ω, treating ω as the frequency
gave the frequency f = 5 Hz instead of the period

follow_ups.S10: ω is measured in rad/s and f in oscillations per second. How many radians does the block go through in one full oscillation?
follow_ups.S9: The mass and spring constant decide ω. If ω is already given, do you still need m to find T?
follow_ups.CORRECT_NO_REASON: You got 0.2 s. Why do we divide 2π by ω instead of just taking 1/ω?
follow_ups.CORRECT: If the same toy is given a block of 4 times the mass, what will its new angular frequency be?
follow_ups.UNCLEAR: Please give one number in seconds for the time of one full oscillation.

twopi.text: used T = 1/ω, leaving out the 2π (treating ω as the frequency)

alternatives.text: worked out the frequency f = ω/2π instead of the period
multiplied by ω instead of dividing (T = 2πω)
used ω = 10, forgetting the π in 10π

steps.text: Link ω to f: ω = 2πf, so f = 10π ÷ 2π = 5 Hz.
steps.trap_text: treating ω itself as the frequency (f = 10π).

steps.text: Period: T = 2π/ω = 2π/(10π) = 0.2 s.
steps.trap_text: using T = 1/ω = 1/(10π) ≈ 0.032 s, leaving out the 2π.

steps.text: Check: T = 1/f = 1/5 = 0.2 s. The question asks for the period, not the 5 Hz frequency.
steps.trap_text: stopping at f = 5 Hz and giving that as the period.

stem: Kavya's spring–mass system oscillates with angular frequency 4π rad/s at an amplitude of 5 cm. She pulls the block to 10 cm and releases it. What is the frequency of oscillation now?

options.B: 2 Hz
options.C: 1 Hz
options.D: 0.5 Hz

r1.text: Frequency is the same thing as omega here, so it is 4π, about 12.6 Hz.

r2.text: f = ω/2π = 2 Hz, and amplitude doesn't change ω for a spring, so it stays 2 Hz.

r3.text: Double the stretch means double the distance, so the period doubles and frequency halves.

calc: f = ω/2π = 4π/2π = 2 Hz, independent of amplitude. S10: f = ω = 4π ≈ 12.6 Hz. S8: T doubled from 0.5 s to 1.0 s → 1 Hz. UNMAPPED: reported T = 0.5 s as 0.5 Hz.

stem: A block on a spring has a time period of 1.2 s. Anjali replaces it with a block 4 times as heavy on the same spring. What is the new time period?

options.B: 1.2 s, unchanged
options.D: It cannot be found without knowing how far the block is pulled before release

r1.text: The spring alone sets the period, so changing the block makes no difference.
